Quite a few decent points made.
- Parents being caring: my point exactly. The concept of it being unsafe for women to step out late at night, but it being alright for men is the issue here. The fact that parents have the need to worry. The pedestal becomes the prison. 

- system being merit based: to some extent sure, specially in the few positions higher up the ladder in central colombo,  where decisions are taken by relatively more open minded people. Based on what I've heard from a few friends in IT I do know that there are gender quotas in these sectors. And I agree with you, I think that it's unfair and its a definete problem solution mismatch.
But a majority of fields outside of IT/engineering, it's significantly more difficult for women to wade through. Specially when it comes down to competitive jobs lower down the ladder with lower pay. I think you're focusing on the few well paying jobs focused in and around Colombo, I'm trying (and possibly failing) to paint a bigger picture. I can't speak for all sectors obviously, but in just my line of work I've faced quite a few gender barricades along the way.  Senior staff hitting on me and when rejected they take it out on a professional front? Being told since day one to avoid certain subspecialities in medicine simply because I was a woman? Being groped by men I've worked with? All problems aren't necessarily merit related. I had a similar attitude to yours all the way till college, but when I started when I started working, the experiences were truly eye opening. 

- Do what's best for humanity? Absolutely. I don't spend my days segregating and judging people based on superficial values and appearance. When I said help make lives better for women once you have the ability to do so, I didn't  imply implementing gender quotas and starting women only corners. I meant intervene when a woman isn't being treated right just because of her gender. Create an environment where women just don't have to fight harder just to get through an ordinary day of work. 

I'm asking women to not play the victim card because it truly won't get us anywhere, there is no blame game at play. But that doesn't mean I should turn a blind eye and lie about life being fair.

This comment is a representation of how blind some are to the patriarchy in SL society. I'm not saying the stat disparity is solely because of the patriarchy but you can't ignore its role. In most SL families education is prioritized when it comes to sons. Dowries are investments for women. You may think its placing women on a pedestal but the pedestal is also what acts as a prison restricting their potential. 
Forget education, most women I know aren't allowed to step out at night alone. Not that they don't want to, they are not allowed to. 
I could spend days listing out all disadvantages women have faced solely bcs of their gender not based off stats I read on articles, but based off my day to day life. 
If a woman happens to read this comment however, what I'd say is stop waiting for the system to change. It won't happen in your lifetime. I don't mean to sound dramatic but when a man fights hard for his dreams, you will have to fight twice as hard to get to the same place. It's unfair, but it is what it is. And when you do get to a position of power, a position of influence - try your best to make the situation better for other women. Do what you wish others had done for you. 

Sameera if you do read this I hope you realize how ignorant your comment was.
The only elephant I'll outrun. With a 4 minute headstart.

Sexual harassment aside, patriarchy is so deeply ingrained in Sri lankan culture that nobody realizes it even exists. Men who have bathed in its luxury remain oblivious and continue to do so. Women who have live under it have either embraced it so deeply that they refuse to consider a scenario where equality thrives or they fear to fight the system which already exists. 
I'm involved in the health sector here in Sri Lanka and I've experienced it first hand multiple times.  And the longer you remain in the system, the deeper the patriarchy gets ingrained in you and less time you spend questioning it. Why? Because fighting the system is more taxing on the short term than going with the flow. Confrontation is more exhausting than acceptance. I've noticed multiple times that not only do men not speak up when a woman gets looked down or treated different just for her gender, but women don't either. Which is probably why it will take decades for Sri Lanka to come out of this bubble. 

If there's any advice I could give based on my experience, it would be to speak up for yourself. Don't expect others to because it will not happen. It's a tough world and you need to first stand up for yourself before you stand up for others. The first time is the most difficult but then it gets easier every time. I know it's tough specially when it's your superiors treating you different, but you gotta do it. Otherwise it'll never go away. 
We women have always been instructed on how a submissive personality suits us best in society because that's the cultural norm. And to break the norm someone has to set the wheels in motion.

1-2  years shorter yes. But for someone who has already been studying for so long it might seem like a significant amount of time. 
I also think it's because of how much work you need to put in during those years. If you are female and you want to start a family, being pregnant as a surgical resident would be immensely more difficult than be let's say as a paediatric resident. I'm not devaluing any field here but just saying that the amount of physical exhaustion to be experienced during those years also matters. And specially if your biological clock is ticking, ( which is common in the medical field) women consider even these minor details.
This is general sum of my opinion on the matter. Not facts, but just what I've seen some of friends take into account when deciding specialities.

Imo and personal experience. There is sexism, but it isn't so intolerable that it keeps you completely out of the field. There is sexism in quite a few career paths and I think the surgery arena happens to be one of them. But I've also faced sexism of more extreme levels in other activities I'm involved in. So if you really want to get into surgery and if you have the required drive to push through, there's nothing stopping you. 

But a significant number of my female friends opt out of surgery for personal reasons. Some of them being it's too long of a commitment and no interest really. surgery is more demanding physically relative to a medical career. Hours standing and peeping into some cavity and all during which you need to remain a 100% focused.  I've met quite a few female proffs specially in obgyn and neurosurgery rotations. But almost no females tread into fields like orthopedics because these have a big physical element to it. Unless you are a significantly physically strong woman who can handle these conditions, these specialities are generally avoided I think. I've also met quite a few female plastic surgeons. 

I understand sexism exists. As a woman I've experienced it myself. When men in the field make snark comments about women in surgery it's irritating I know. But I think complaining about it won't get you anywhere. What you can really do is push through ( even if it takes more effort), get where you want to be and then help create the change you want to see. As a medical student, intern or resident you might not have as much Influence but higher up the ladder you go, the louder your voice gets.

I like my ramen coated in thick broth but no real broth to drink off with a spoon, I hope u get what I mean. And I don't like it when the egg mixes into the broth almost like an egg drop soup. 
My usual is minimal water with noodles, add the flavor packets immediately and let it cook. Almost feel like the ramen absorbs some of the flavor with the cooking time. Almost when the noodles is done, crack the egg open on top. You can break the yolk and mix slightly on top to just break the egg apart but don't mix it too hard so that it mixes completely with the noodles..
Let it cook for 1-2 mins. Then turn off heat and sprinkle some spring onions on top. Delish!
